description: We’re a 5-person Charlotte team building a Space Mission Design Game where real NASA data decides if your mission succeeds. We have 3 coders, 1 designers/video creator, 2 presenters, plus a clear plan and roles. Join us to build a real, playable game with NASA data. We have 1 spot open and want someone into data, math, or physics to turn NASA numbers like distance, gravity, and fuel into game rules. Space science or sound design is a plus!
summary: Space Mission Design Game is a free desktop game for Windows and macOS where players design, launch and fly a real space mission, then find out exactly why it succeeded or failed. Players choose a destination, launch vehicle, spacecraft parts and science instruments while balancing budget, mass, power, communications and orbital constraints. Every number is tied to a credited source, including NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool, NASA's Small Spacecraft Technology report and the real Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter mission, so players learn the same trade-offs real mission engineers face. Sandbox mode removes the limits so beginners can explore any planet, and an end-of-mission report explains every failure so players can fix it and fly again. Every choice has a cost.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Space Mission Design Game is a free desktop game where you plan a real space mission from concept to operation. You pick a destination, a launch vehicle, a spacecraft bus, power, communications and science instruments, all while staying inside a real budget and mass limit. Then you launch, fly the mission and get a report that explains exactly what worked and what failed. HOW IT WORKS 1. Choose Sandbox (no limits, any planet) or a Mission with real constraints. 2. Build the spacecraft: every part changes cost, mass and power, and the game shows the trade-off live. 3. Launch and watch the simulation. Events such as a solar flare warning force real-time decisions. 4. Read the mission report: it scores science return, budget and risk, and explains every failure. Costs and performance are based on credited sources, including NASA GMAT, NASA's State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology report and NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, so the numbers reflect real missions. BENEFITS AND IMPACT Students rarely get to try a whole mission from start to finish. This game makes those trade-offs concrete. It is free, runs offline on Windows and macOS, needs no account, and starts at a beginner level, so anyone can think like a mission engineer. The scoring is fully open and every number is tied to a credited source, so players can trust what they learn. Failing is part of the design: the report explains exactly why a mission failed so players fix it and fly again. TOOLS Python 3.13 (standard library for all game logic), CustomTkinter for the interface, a pure-Python 3D canvas engine for the mission view (no game engine or GPU needed), Pillow for planet artwork, NASA GMAT R2016a for astrodynamics, PyInstaller for the Windows .exe and macOS .dmg, and GitHub Actions to build and publish releases automatically. WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE Instead of a quiz, players own real decisions with real consequences, live. The same seed re-run makes cause and effect visible, and Sandbox mode lets players experiment freely before taking on a real mission. FUTURE More scenarios out to dwarf planets like Pluto and Ceres, checks that flight paths do not conflict with planets' moons, and fixes from every playtest. Product blueprint: https://tharunj-web.github.io/frontier6-presentation/blueprint 3D MODELS: Some 3D models in the game were sourced from free online model libraries; the specific sources are being confirmed.
